items.title: One-charge soft photon count example
items.statement:
Use the one-charge prescribed current of
[[pthm-qft-example-soft-coherent-counts]] with final velocity
$v=\tfrac12$ along $\hat{\mathbf z}$. Choose any upper photon-energy cutoff
$\Lambda>0$ in joules and set $\lambda=\Lambda/\mathrm e$, where $\mathrm e$
is Euler's number. The angular coefficient is
$$C=\frac{\alpha}{\pi}(2\log 3-2)>0.$$
The exact cutoff coherent state therefore has mean photon count $C$, vacuum
probability $e^{-C}$, and mean photon energy
$C\Lambda(1-\mathrm e^{-1})$ joules. Each halving of $\lambda$ increases the
mean count by $C\log 2$; the mean energy remains bounded and tends to
$C\Lambda$ as $\lambda\downarrow0$. These are model predictions for the
prepared free state.

items.title: Fan2022 reported electron magnetic-moment determination
items.statement:
The authors report the weighted average of eleven cavity-corrected
determinations:
$$-\frac{\mu}{\mu_B}=\frac{g}{2}=1.00115965218059(13).$$
They state that the parenthetical digits give a $1\sigma$ uncertainty of
$1.3\times10^{-13}$ in this dimensionless ratio. The reported consistency
across the eleven field settings is a source observation; this item does not
turn it into a proof of QED or of the apparatus model.

The raw trials, covariance matrix, and weights are not reconstructed here.

items.title: Qualified reported anomaly by exact affine subtraction
items.statement:
Let the source-reported dimensionless ratio be denoted
$\widehat{g_s/2}:=-\widehat\mu/\mu_B$, where $\mu_B=e\hbar/(2m)$ is the
Bohr magneton, with $e>0$ the elementary-charge magnitude in coulombs,
$\hbar$ the reduced Planck constant in joule-seconds, and $m>0$ the electron
rest mass in kilograms, as specified in
[[exp-qft-fan-electron-moment-2022]]. The hat marks an empirical estimate,
not an exact constant.
Define the derived dimensionless anomaly estimate
$\widehat a_e:=\widehat{g_s/2}-1$. Under the empirical premise from
[[exp-qft-fan-electron-moment-2022]], whose reported central value is
$\widehat{g_s/2}=1.00115965218059$, exact subtraction gives
$$\widehat a_e=0.00115965218059.$$
The source-stated $1\sigma$ uncertainty remains $1.3\times10^{-13}$, and all
apparatus, correction, weighting, correlation, and source-data qualifications
of the experiment remain in force. This is only an affine transformation of a
reported estimate; it supplies no comparison with a theoretical prediction.

items.title: Exact real scalar free model
items.design_state: Exact real scalar specialization with explicit shell, Fock domain and vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonian; conditional on the QFT-F01 physical adoption.
items.physical_scope: One real scalar species in four-dimensional flat Minkowski spacetime, with the adopted bosonic Fock representation, inverse-length parameter μ≥0, and exact vacuum-subtracted Hamiltonian ℏc dΓs(ωμ). This definition supplies no interacting term, regulator, point-field product, or empirical universality claim.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], as in the inspected Fock
construction.

Select the real-scalar branch of the QFT-F01 physical adoption
[[post-qft-free-field-model]]: one real spin-zero species with bosonic
statistics and the zero-particle vacuum. For a smooth real classical field
$\phi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R$ of canonical length degree $-1$,
that postulate adopts the local action density represented by
$$\frac{S_\phi}{\hbar}=-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4} \left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi_{\mathrm n}\partial_b\phi_{\mathrm n} +\mu^2\phi_{\mathrm n}^2\right)\,d^4x.$$
The total action is defined by this integral when its density is integrable;
it need not converge for an arbitrary smooth global field. For a real
$h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4)$ and $\epsilon\in\mathbb R$, the normalized
action difference under $\phi_{\mathrm n}\mapsto\phi_{\mathrm n}+\epsilon h$
is defined by integrating the difference of the displayed densities. That
difference is smooth and supported in $\operatorname{supp}h$, so its integral
is finite even when neither total action exists. Only these compactly
supported variations are used, as in [[post-qft-free-field-model]].
The species, statistics, state, and local action density are physical model inputs. The
present item fixes the exact flat-spacetime free Fock model to which the
later deductions apply.

Use the oriented and time-oriented Minkowski spacetime, signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and length coordinates $x^0=ct$ and
$\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$ from [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Write
$\Box=-\partial_0^2+\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_j^2$. Choose an inverse-length
parameter $\mu\ge0$. When $\mu>0$, the corresponding SI rest mass is
$m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}=\hbar\mu/c>0$; $\mu=0$ denotes the massless branch and
assigns no positive rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, put
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$, with units
$\mathrm m^{-1}$.

Let $H_\mu^+$, $d\nu_\mu$, $H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C)$, and
$K_\mu:\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)\to H_\mu$ be the future mass shell, measure,
one-particle Hilbert space, and Fourier restriction of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. In the massless case the null apex is omitted;
it has measure zero. The shell measure is
$d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))$.

Use the symmetric bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$, vacuum
$\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$, and dense finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ from
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The Fock pairing is linear in its second
variable. Creation $a^\dagger(h)$ is linear in $h$, while annihilation $a(h)$
is conjugate-linear in $h$. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)$ define the
complex-linear smeared scalar field on $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ by

$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$

For real $f$, this is the symmetric scalar field whose self-adjoint closure
and bounded Weyl functions are constructed in
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. A smeared field is a domain-qualified
operator-valued distribution; the item introduces no pointwise operator
$\Phi_\mu(x)$.

Define $d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu)$ on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication
by $\sum_{r=1}^n\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r)$, with value zero on the vacuum
sector. The exact maximal domain is

$$D(d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu))= \left\{\Psi:\sum_{n\ge1}\int_{(H_\mu^+)^n} \left|\sum_{r=1}^n\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r)\right|^2 |\Psi_n(\mathbf k_1,\ldots,\mathbf k_n)|^2\,d\nu_\mu^n<\infty\right\}.$$

The physical Hamiltonian of this selected model is the vacuum-subtracted
self-adjoint operator
$H_\mu^{\mathrm{phys}}=\hbar c\,d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu)$ on that domain, as
defined by the multiplier construction of
[[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. It has units of joules and
$H_\mu^{\mathrm{phys}}\Omega=0$. No infinite zero-point-energy sum is part of
this definition. The canonical scalar engineering dimension is
$\mathrm m^{-1}$; a spacetime test function of unit $\mathrm m^{-3}$ makes the
smeared field dimensionless, consistently with
[[def-qft-framework-units]].

items.design_state: Complete conditional deductions for the real scalar model: Klein-Gordon equation, covariance, forward spectrum, exact mass gap, and local Weyl commutativity.
items.physical_scope: Conditional properties of the selected four-dimensional real scalar free Fock model: the smeared Klein–Gordon field, proper orthochronous Poincare covariance, vacuum and forward-cone spectrum, exact mass gap, and isotony and spacelike commutativity of bounded local Weyl algebras.
items.statement:
Assume the scalar model adoption planned in
[[post-qft-free-field-model]] and Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu\ge0$ and use the model, shell, field,
vacuum, and units of [[def-qft-free-scalar-model]] and
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. These are conditional model deductions, with no
empirical premise.

For every Schwartz test $f$, $\Phi_\mu(f)$ is defined on
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{fin}}$; for real $f$ it is symmetric and essentially
self-adjoint there. Distributionally,
$\Phi_\mu((\Box-\mu^2)f)=0$. The Fock lift of the proper orthochronous
Poincare action is unitary, leaves $\Omega$ invariant, and implements
covariance of the smeared field. For real Schwartz tests the vacuum
two-point form is $\langle\Omega,\Phi_\mu(f)\Phi_\mu(g)\Omega\rangle=\langle K_\mu f,K_\mu g\rangle_2$, and it is nonnegative when $g=f$. The
joint spectrum of spacetime translations is contained in the closed forward
cone.

For real compactly supported smooth tests with pairwise spacelike-separated
supports, the smeared fields commute on $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{fin}}$. The
bounded local Weyl algebras are isotonic and algebras for spacelike-separated
regions commute. The physical Hamiltonian is self-adjoint on the exact
multiplier domain in [[def-qft-free-scalar-model]], is nonnegative, and has
zero-energy eigenspace $\ker H_\mu^{\mathrm{phys}}=\mathbb C\Omega$.
Thus its normalized zero-energy vectors are $e^{i\theta}\Omega$ for
$\theta\in\mathbb R$. If $\mu>0$, the infimum of its
positive spectrum is $\hbar c\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c^2$. If $\mu=0$, its
positive spectrum has no gap above zero.

items.statement:
Assume the scalar model adoption planned in
[[post-qft-free-field-model]], Countable Choice
[[def-countable-choice]], and the exact model of
[[def-qft-free-scalar-model]]. For real Schwartz tests $f_1,\ldots,f_n$,
the vacuum expectation of the ordered product of smeared fields is zero
when $n$ is odd. When $n$ is even, it is the sum over pairings of products
of the corresponding two-point functions
$\langle K_\mu f_r,K_\mu f_s\rangle_2$ for $r<s$ in each pair. For a real
Schwartz test $f$, the bounded Weyl operator has vacuum expectation
$\langle\Omega,W_\mu(f)\Omega\rangle
=\exp(-\|K_\mu f\|_2^2/2)$.

The time-ordered two-point carrier is the tempered distribution $H_\mu$
defined by the partial spatial Fourier formula of
[[lem-qft-free-time-ordered-kernel]]. It agrees with the ordered Wightman
distributions away from equal-time coincidence and satisfies
$(\Box-\mu^2)H_\mu=i\delta_0$. The formula fixes its extension at coincidence
and includes no additional prefactor $i$. These are conditional deductions
for the selected free model.

items.title: Exact Dirac particle/antiparticle free model
items.statement:
Fix the oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski spacetime and inertial length coordinates of [[def-qft-framework-units]], with $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $x^0=ct$. The parameter $\mu\ge0$ and wave vector $\mathbf k$ have unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$; $\omega(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$ also has unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$. For $\mu>0$, $\mu=m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c/\hbar$; $\mu=0$ is the admitted massless branch. The corresponding SI energy and momentum are $\hbar c\omega$ joules and $\hbar\mathbf k$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The canonically normalized Dirac field has engineering length degree $-3/2$; a spacetime spinor test has degree $-5/2$, making its spacetime-smearing pairing dimensionless. These are the unit conventions of [[def-qft-framework-units]], not claims about interacting-field scaling.

Adopt the Dirac branch of [[post-qft-free-field-model]]: one free Dirac species, the selected CAR representation and zero-particle vacuum are physical model assumptions. Countable Choice is the mathematical choice strength used by the Fock construction [[def-countable-choice]].

Use $\mathbb C^4$ spinors and the matrices, mass-shell parameter, one-particle Hilbert space $\mathcal H_D$, multiplier $h_D(\mathbf k)=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf k+\beta\mu$, projections $P_\pm(\mathbf k)$ and propagator $W_D$ defined in [[def-qft-dirac-projections]]. The mathematical supplier [[lem-qft-dirac-projection-matrices]] establishes that $P_\pm$ are complementary orthogonal projections of rank two, that $\mathcal H_\pm=\operatorname{ran}P_\pm$ are closed, and that $h_D$ is self-adjoint on its maximal multiplication domain. The one-particle space of the adopted field is
$$\mathcal K_D=\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-},$$
where the bar denotes the conjugate Hilbert space. Its fermionic Fock space, vacuum and creation/annihilation maps use [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]] and [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]].

For a Schwartz spinor test $F\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C^4)$, set
$$\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x}F(t,\mathbf x)\,d^3\mathbf x,\qquad u_F(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R}W_D(t,\mathbf k)\widehat F(t,\mathbf k)\,dt.$$
The physical field is the bounded smeared map
$$\Psi(F)=c(P_+u_F)+c^\dagger(\overline{P_-u_F}),$$
with the exact test-map and CAR construction of [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]]. It is antilinear in $F$. Its positive-energy branch is the particle annihilation term; the conjugate negative-energy branch occurs as antiparticle creation. This is a model assignment: it does not identify negative-energy Fock excitations with physical states, invoke a filled Dirac sea, or prove the general spin-statistics theorem. No pointwise field operator is defined here.

items.title: Dirac CAR, covariance, graded locality and positive Fock energy
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and the adopted Dirac branch of [[post-qft-free-field-model]] as specified by [[def-qft-free-dirac-model]]. For all Schwartz spinor tests $F,G$, the bounded smeared field $\Psi$ is antilinear in its test, satisfies
$$\{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)\}=0,\qquad \{\Psi(F),\Psi(G)^\dagger\}=\langle u_F,u_G\rangle I,$$
and solves the tested free Dirac equation. If $F$ and $G$ have compact spacelike-separated supports, the field-field and field-adjoint anticommutators vanish; consequently, finite even polynomials in the bounded smeared fields commute across spacelike-separated regions.

Let $\widetilde G_D$ be the translation and explicit spin-lift group defined in [[lem-qft-dirac-covariance-spectrum]]. Its strongly continuous unitary Fock representation $U$ satisfies
$$U(\widetilde g)\Psi(F)U(\widetilde g)^{-1}=\Psi(\tau_{\widetilde g}F),\qquad \tau_{\widetilde g}F(x)=(S^{-1})^\dagger F(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a)),$$
for $\widetilde g=(a,\Lambda,S)$. For the explicit spatial rotation lift, $S_R(2\pi)=-I_4$ and $S_R(4\pi)=I_4$; hence the $2\pi$ test pullback is $F\mapsto-F$ and $U_{2\pi}\Psi(F)U_{2\pi}^{-1}=-\Psi(F)$, while the $4\pi$ test pullback and field action are identities. The vacuum is invariant and cyclic for the global graded field algebra. On the $n$-particle sector, $U_{2\pi}=(-1)^n I$ and $U_{4\pi}=I$.

The joint spectrum of translations lies in the closed future cone. If $K_D$ denotes the length-coordinate time-translation generator of [[lem-qft-dirac-covariance-spectrum]], its zero-energy eigenspace is $\ker K_D=\mathbb C\Omega$, where $\Omega$ is the normalized vacuum; thus normalized zero-energy vectors differ from $\Omega$ only by a complex phase. For $\mu>0$, the nonvacuum spectrum has gap at least $\mu$ in inverse-length units, hence $m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}c^2$ in SI energy units. The physical energy is $H_D^{\mathrm{SI}}=\hbar cK_D\ge0$ on the same domain and has the same kernel. This Fock generator acts on a different Hilbert space from the first-quantized multiplier $h_D$, which has both signs of energy. These are conditional deductions in the adopted model, not empirical claims.

items.statement: Define $\mathcal A_D^{\mathrm{even}}$ as the norm closure of finite linear combinations of the identity and even-degree products of $\Psi(F)$ and $\Psi(F)^\dagger$, for Schwartz spinor tests $F$. In the selected free Dirac model, let $U_{2\pi}$ implement a spatial rotation by $2\pi$ and let $U_{4\pi}$ implement a rotation by $4\pi$. On the $n$-particle sector of the adopted antisymmetric Fock decomposition, indexed by $n\in\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$, $U_{2\pi}$ acts as $(-1)^n$ times the identity; $U_{4\pi}=I$. Every finite even polynomial in bounded spacetime-smeared Dirac fields and their adjoints is invariant under conjugation by $U_{2\pi}$, and therefore so is $\mathcal A_D^{\mathrm{even}}$. This is an exact model calculation; it does not infer a general spin-statistics theorem.

items.title: Free observable domains and limits of point notation
items.design_state: Develops exact operator domains and moments, locality of the selected bounded scalar and even Dirac observable algebras, and the precise limits of Gaussian point-smearing notation. The Born interpretation is conditional on a constructed instrument; point fields and coincident products are not supplied.
items.physical_scope: The selected flat four-dimensional real scalar bosonic and Dirac CAR Fock models, with their chosen vacua and bounded smeared observable algebras. Operator-domain and point-smearing conclusions are conditional on the named mathematical carriers. No interacting theory, pointwise field operator, coincident product, thermal trace, apparatus, or empirical outcome is asserted.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice, $\mu\ge0$, and the selected free-field model of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]]. Use the four-dimensional affine Minkowski chart,
signature $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, length coordinate $x^0=ct$,
and inverse-length parameter $\mu$ of [[def-qft-framework-units]]. For an open
region $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, use the scalar and Dirac test functions and
bounded local observable algebras defined in
[[def-qft-free-field-observables]]: scalar tests are real members of
$C_c^\infty(O)$, Dirac tests are members of
$C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb C^4)$, and the Dirac observable algebra is generated by
even products of bounded smeared CAR fields and their adjoints.

For a real Schwartz scalar test $f$, the closure of $\Phi_\mu(f)$ is
self-adjoint on its exact Segal-field multiplier domain. The scalar number,
Hamiltonian and momentum operators and the Dirac Hamiltonian and momentum
operators have the exact maximal sector-sum domains stated in
[[lem-qft-free-domain-observables]]. In particular,
$$D(N_s)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
If $A$ is one of these self-adjoint operators and $\Psi$ is normalized with
$\Psi\in D(A)$, then its model mean $\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle$ and variance
$$\operatorname{Var}_\Psi(A)=\|(A-\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle)\Psi\|^2$$
are finite; this needs $\Psi\in D(A)$, not $\Psi\in D(A^2)$. The product
$AB\Psi$ is defined only when $\Psi\in D(B)$ and $B\Psi\in D(A)$.

If $O_1,O_2$ are open regions and
$\eta_{ab}(x-y)^a(x-y)^b>0$ for every $x\in O_1$ and $y\in O_2$, then the
scalar Weyl algebras of the two regions commute, and the even local Dirac
algebras of the two regions commute. These are algebraic properties of the
specified free representations.

The chosen construction supplies only test-smeared fields and does not define
$\Phi_\mu(x)$, $\Psi(x)$, or coincident diagonal products. Fix a point
$x_0\in\mathbb R^4$ and a nonnegative Schwartz function
$\rho\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ with $\int\rho(y)\,d^4y=1$. For each
width $\epsilon>0$ measured in metres, put
$\rho_{\epsilon,x_0}(x)=\epsilon^{-4}\rho((x-x_0)/\epsilon)$. The rescaled
coordinate is dimensionless, so $\rho_{\epsilon,x_0}$ has unit
$\mathrm m^{-4}$. These tests
converge on Schwartz tests to the point-evaluation functional
$\delta_{x_0}(g):=g(x_0)$, but
$\|\Phi_\mu(\rho_{\epsilon,x_0})\Omega\|\to\infty$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.
For the bounded equal-time CAR field $\Psi_t(u)$ defined in
[[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]], fix a spinor $z\in\mathbb C^4$ with
$z^\dagger z=1$ and a nonnegative Schwartz function
$\sigma\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^3)$ with
$\int\sigma(y)\,d^3y=1$, and put
$u_{\epsilon,x_0}(\mathbf x)=\epsilon^{-3}
\sigma((\mathbf x-\mathbf x_0)/\epsilon)z$ with the same width $\epsilon$.
The spatial rescaled coordinate is dimensionless and $u_{\epsilon,x_0}$ has
unit $\mathrm m^{-3}$. These tests approximate a
spatial point evaluation $h\mapsto z^\dagger h(x_0)$ for each
$h\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$. Write
$\mathcal F_D:=\mathcal F_a(\mathcal H_+\oplus\overline{\mathcal H_-})$
for the Dirac Fock space of [[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]], and define
$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup\{\|A\xi\|: \xi\in\mathcal F_D,\ \|\xi\|=1\}$
for each bounded linear operator $A:\mathcal F_D\to\mathcal F_D$. For each
fixed coordinate time $t$ in seconds,
$\|\Psi_t(u_{\epsilon,x_0})\|_{\mathrm{op}}\to\infty$. Neither
family has a finite limit in its respective Fock or operator-norm topology.
This restriction does not rule out other distributional or renormalized
constructions. The Born interpretation of
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]] applies only after a density
state and normalized finite bounded instrument have actually been supplied;
this item reports no apparatus or outcome.

items.title: Classical equations and adopted exact free quantum representation
items.design_state: Checks the classical compact-variation scalar and Dirac equations against the tested equations of the separately adopted free representations. Quantization and statistics assignments are model assumptions, not deductions from the classical actions.
items.physical_scope: The selected flat four-dimensional free real scalar and Dirac models, with the stated (-+++) signature, inverse-length mass parameter and chosen Fock representations. The result matches compact-variation classical equations with weak test equations of the adopted representations. It does not derive quantization, a general spin-statistics rule, interacting dynamics, empirical validity, or a measurement outcome.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and the selected free-field model of
[[post-qft-free-field-model]], using the metric, length coordinates, inverse-
length parameter $\mu\ge0$, field dimensions and Clifford convention fixed by
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. The classical scalar field
$\phi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R$ is smooth and real; the classical
Dirac field $\psi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb C^4$ is smooth with
commuting components. Their adopted free actions are the scalar and Dirac
functionals stated in [[post-qft-free-field-model]]. Action symbols are used
only through compactly supported smooth variations, so no global
integrability of the classical background fields is assumed.

The compact-variation stationarity equations are
$$(\Box-\mu^2)\phi_{\mathrm n}=0,\qquad (i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu)\psi_{\mathrm n}=0,$$
with $\Box=-\partial_0^2+\Delta_{\mathbf x}$. In the separately adopted
scalar and Dirac Fock representations, the corresponding weak test equations
are, for $f\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$ and
$F\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C^4)$,
$$\Phi_\mu((\Box-\mu^2)f)=0,\qquad \Psi\!\left((i\partial_0-h_D(-i\nabla))F\right)=0.$$
Here “weak test equation” means precisely that smearing the constructed field
with the displayed differential operator gives the zero operator on its
stated common domain. With $h_D(\mathbf k)=\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot\mathbf k+\beta\mu$,
$\gamma^0=\beta$, and $\gamma^j=\beta\alpha^j$ as adopted in
[[post-qft-free-field-model]], the Dirac test operator is equivalent to
$i\gamma^a\partial_a-\mu$.

Thus the classical action equations and the tested equations of the selected
free representations have the same differential expressions at these
normalizations. The Fock representation, species/statistics assignments and
vacua are additional physical model assumptions; they are not deductions from
the classical actions. No empirical outcome or measurement is asserted.

items.title: The specified Gaussian family has no finite vacuum-vector norm limit
items.design_state: Refutes the finite vacuum-vector norm-limit claim for the specified normalized scalar Gaussian spacetime-smearing family; it does not exclude other distributional or renormalized constructions.
items.physical_scope: The normalized Gaussian spacetime-smearing family for the real scalar field in the selected four-dimensional free Fock vacuum. It refutes only convergence in this representation's vacuum-vector norm; distributional or renormalized point-field constructions in other senses are outside scope. No empirical observation is asserted.
items.statement:
Assume all hypotheses of
[[pthm-qft-free-observable-domain-limits]], including Countable Choice and the
selected four-dimensional free real scalar Fock model with $\mu\ge0$. A
normalized Gaussian profile on dimensionless $\mathbb R^d$ means
$$g(y)=\frac{\sqrt{\det Q}}{(2\pi)^{d/2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac12(y-m)^TQ(y-m)\right),$$
where $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Q$ is a dimensionless real symmetric
positive-definite matrix. Fix $x_0\in\mathbb R^4$ and such a profile
$\rho\in\mathscr S(\mathbb R^4)$. For a width $\epsilon>0$ measured in
metres, put $\rho_{\epsilon,x_0}(x)=\epsilon^{-4}
\rho((x-x_0)/\epsilon)$. The claim
that $\Phi_\mu(\rho_{\epsilon,x_0})\Omega$ converges in Fock norm to a finite
vector as $\epsilon\downarrow0$, thereby defining a sharp point field on the
vacuum by this norm limit, is false.

items.title: Finite-lattice polynomial Hamiltonian data
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). A **finite-mode regulator** in this item is a fixed
finite nonempty label set $J$ with $N:=|J|\ge1$, a fixed enumeration of $J$ by
$\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and the real coordinate vector
$q=(q_1,\ldots,q_N)\in\mathbb R^N$. The labels may name sites of a finite
lattice or finitely many modes; their geometry enters only through the chosen
polynomial below. No limit in $N$ is part of this definition.

Choose real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$, constants $c>0$ and $C_0\ge0$,
and a real polynomial $V\in\mathbb R[q_1,\ldots,q_N]$ such that
$$V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0\qquad(q\in\mathbb R^N).$$
Let $H_N:=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, with vectors identified up to almost
everywhere equality and inner product
$$\langle u,v\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb R^N}u(q)\overline{v(q)}\,dq,$$
linear in the first variable. Under Countable Choice this is a complex Hilbert
space by [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Let
$D_0:=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, the smooth compactly supported
complex-valued functions. The associated **polynomial differential expression**
is the map
$$h_0:D_0\to H_N,\qquad h_0u:=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Vu.$$
It is well defined because each derivative of $u$ and the product $Vu$ are
smooth and compactly supported. Set $W:=V+C_0+1$, so
$W(q)\ge1+c|q|^2$. This definition specifies finite mathematical data and a
differential expression; it does not choose a self-adjoint operator domain or
assert a continuum or infinite-volume limit.
items.strategy: Definition; no proof supplied.

references.title: Gerald Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, 2nd ed., §§2.3 and 8.3, pp.76–83 and 212–214
Richard S. Laugesen, Spectral Theory of Partial Differential Equations — Lecture Notes, Chapter 8, pp.48–50

items.title: Coercive polynomial form completion and injection
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Since $W+1\ge2$ and every $a_j>0$, $a$ is a Hermitian positive-definite sesquilinear form on $D_0$: in particular $a(u,u)=\sum_j a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2\ge2\|u\|_2^2$, and $a(u,u)=0$ forces $u=0$ in $H_N$. Thus its Cauchy-sequence completion with the stated equivalence relation is a well-defined inner-product space. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 To see that the completion is complete, let $(X_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence of its classes. By [A1], choose $u_n\in D_0$ with $\|[u_n]-X_n\|_Q<2^{-n}$ for each $n$. The triangle inequality makes $(u_n)$ $Q$-Cauchy; its class $X$ is defined by the Cauchy-sequence construction, and $\|X_n-X\|_Q\le2^{-n}+\|[u_n]-X\|_Q\to0$. Hence $Q$ is complete and therefore Hilbert. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a $Q$-Cauchy representative sequence $(u_n)$, the inequalities $\|u_n-u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, $\sqrt{a_j}\|\partial_j u_n-\partial_j u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, and $\|\sqrt{W+1}(u_n-u_m)\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$ show that $u_n$, each $\partial_j u_n$, and $\sqrt{W+1}u_n$ converge in $L^2$ by [F2]; write their limits as $u$, $g_j$, and $h$. The first limit defines a continuous map $Q\to H_N$, since $\|u\|_2\le\|[u_n]\|_Q$, and equivalent Cauchy sequences have the same $L^2$ limit. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 For every $\varphi\in D_0$, integration by parts gives $\int u_n\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int (\partial_j u_n)\overline\varphi$. Passing to the limit in both integrals by $L^2$ convergence and Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\int u\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$, so $g_j$ is the stated weak derivative. [step 2.2, F2, F3, algebra]

3.2 On each compact ball $B_R$, the continuous polynomial $W+1$ is bounded. Therefore $\sqrt{W+1}u_n\to\sqrt{W+1}u$ in $L^2(B_R)$, while the same sequence converges there to $h$; uniqueness of limits gives $h=\sqrt{W+1}u$ almost everywhere on every integer-radius ball and hence almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^N$. Taking limits of the component norms in $a(u_n,u_n)$ now gives the displayed formula for $\|u\|_Q^2$. [step 2.2, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 If $u=0$ in $L^2$, then step 3.1 says $\langle g_j,\varphi\rangle=0$ for every $\varphi\in D_0$; this pairing is continuous by [F3] and $D_0$ is dense by [F4], so it vanishes on all of $H_N$, and taking $\varphi=g_j$ gives $g_j=0$. Step 3.2 then gives $h=0$; the norm formula yields $\|[u_n]\|_Q=0$, so the embedding is injective. Finally its image contains $D_0$, which is dense in $H_N$ by [F4]; thus the continuous injection has dense image and all claims follow. [step 3.1, step 3.2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

Richard S. Laugesen, Spectral Theory of Partial Differential Equations — Lecture Notes, Chapters 4 and 8, pp.27–32 and 48–50

items.title: Cube mean estimate and compact form inclusion
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume the finite-dimensional coercive form data and Hilbert space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]. The inclusion
$J:Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ is compact: the closure in $H_N$ of the image of
every bounded subset of $Q$ is compact in the metric topology. The proof below
uses an explicit cube-mean approximation for each finite $N$ and does not
assume a general Rellich theorem.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** Countable Choice as inherited through [F1], the finite data, and an arbitrary $Q$-bounded set.

1.1 Let $C$ be a cube of side $\delta>0$ and $u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$, with $u_C:=|C|^{-1}\int_Cu$. Expanding the square and using Fubini on the finite cube gives
$$\int_C|u-u_C|^2=\frac1{2|C|}\int_C\int_C|u(x)-u(y)|^2\,dx\,dy.$$
Telescope $u(x)-u(y)$ through the $N$ coordinate changes and use $|\sum_{j=1}^Nz_j|^2\le N\sum_j|z_j|^2$. For the $j$th change, the fundamental theorem of calculus and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|D_j(x,y)|^2\le\delta\int_{\min(x_j,y_j)}^{\max(x_j,y_j)}|\partial_ju|^2$. For fixed values of the other coordinates and fixed $s\in[0,\delta]$, the measure of pairs $(x_j,y_j)$ whose segment contains $s$ is $2s(\delta-s)\le\delta^2/2$; integrating the displayed bound over the cube variables and dividing by $2|C|$ therefore yields the safe estimate
$$\|u-u_C\|_{L^2(C)}^2\le N\delta^2\sum_{j=1}^N\|\partial_j u\|_{L^2(C)}^2.$$
It applies to complex $u$ because the squared-modulus Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is used. [F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 For $R>0$ and $u\in Q$, the coercive weight gives
$$\int_{|q|>R}|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\int_{|q|>R}c|q|^2|u(q)|^2\,dq\le\frac1{cR^2}\|u\|_Q^2.$$
Thus the $L^2$ tails of the $Q$ unit ball are uniformly small for large $R$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The estimate of step 1.1 passes to every $u\in Q$: approximate $u$ in the $Q$ norm by elements of $C_c^\infty$ (the defining completion), restrict to $C$, and use [F1] to pass the $L^2$ and derivative limits. [step 1.1, F1]

3.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $R$ so the squared tail in step 1.2 is below $\varepsilon^2/16$. For the $Q$ unit ball, [F1] gives $\sum_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2\le\sum_j a_j^{-1}$. Choose an integer $M$ large enough that $\delta:=2R/M$ satisfies $N\delta^2\sum_j a_j^{-1}<\varepsilon^2/16$, and partition $[-R,R]^N$ into the resulting finitely many cubes of side $\delta$. Summing the squared estimates of step 2.1 over these disjoint cubes bounds the total mean-approximation error by $N\delta^2\sum_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2<\varepsilon^2/16$. The squared error outside $[-R,R]^N$ is the tail from step 1.2; thus replacing $u$ on each cube by its mean and setting it to zero outside the large cube has total squared $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon^2/8$, hence norm error below $\varepsilon/2$. [step 2.1, step 1.2, F1, choose, algebra]

4.1 For the finite partition in step 3.1, the piecewise-constant mean function $m_u$ satisfies $\|m_u\|_2^2=\sum_C|C||u_C|^2\le\sum_C\|u\|_{L^2(C)}^2\le\|u\|_2^2\le1$ by Cauchy--Schwarz [F3]. Thus each mean coordinate has modulus at most $|C|^{-1/2}$, so the vectors of means lie in a bounded box in a finite-dimensional complex coordinate space. Subdivide its real-and-imaginary coordinates into finitely many boxes of sufficiently small side length so that the associated piecewise-constant functions approximate every mean vector to $L^2$ error below $\varepsilon/2$. Combining with step 3.1 gives a finite $\varepsilon$-net for the image of the $Q$ unit ball. Scaling shows that the image of every bounded $Q$ set is totally bounded. [step 3.1, F1, F3, algebra]

5.1 Let $K$ be the $H_N$ closure of the image of the $Q$ unit ball. It is complete because it is closed in the complete space $H_N$ [F1]. Suppose an open cover of $K$ has no finite subcover. For each $n\ge1$, step 4.1 supplies a finite $2^{-n-2}$-net for the image of the $Q$ unit ball with centers in $H_N$; the corresponding closed balls of radius $2^{-n-1}$ cover its closure $K$. Starting with $C_0=K$, choose the least ball index for which $C_n:=C_{n-1}\cap\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$ has no finite subcover. Such an index exists, since otherwise finitely many finite subcovers would cover $C_{n-1}$. Each $C_n$ is nonempty, closed, nested, and has diameter at most $2^{-n}$. For $m>n$, any point of nonempty $C_m$ lies in both selected balls, so $\|p_m-p_n\|_2\le2^{-m-1}+2^{-n-1}$; hence $(p_n)$ is Cauchy and converges to some $p\in H_N$. Since $C_n$ is nonempty and is contained in both $K$ and $\overline B(p_n,2^{-n-1})$, the distance from $p_n$ to $K$ is at most $2^{-n-1}$. Therefore $\operatorname{dist}(p,K)\le\|p-p_n\|_2+2^{-n-1}\to0$; closedness of $K$ gives $p\in K$. For fixed $n$ and every $m>n$, nonempty $C_m\subseteq C_n$ has a point $y\in C_m$ with $\|p_m-y\|_2\le2^{-m-1}$. Thus there are points of $C_n$ arbitrarily close to $p$, and closedness gives $p\in C_n$. An open set of the cover containing $p$ contains $K\cap B(p,r)$ for some $r>0$; for large $n$, $\operatorname{diam}(C_n)<r$, so that one open set covers $C_n$, a contradiction. Thus $K$ is compact. All recursive ball choices are least admissible indices in finite lists. [step 4.1, F1, algebra]

6.1 Step 5.1 proves that the closed-unit-ball image under $J$ has compact closure; applying the equivalent criterion in [F2] to the linear inclusion proves that $J:Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ is compact. [step 5.1, F2] ∎

items.title: Anisotropic Hermite oscillator and quadratic form basis
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** the oscillator form, its completion, and positive coefficients $a_j,c$.

1.1 In [F2] choose $\hbar=1$, $m_j=(2a_j)^{-1}$ and $\omega_j=2\sqrt{a_jc}$. Then $\hbar^2/(2m_j)=a_j$ and $m_j\omega_j^2/2=c$. The eigenvalue from [F2] in coordinate $j$ is $\omega_j(n_j+1/2)=(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}$. Summing over the $N$ coordinates gives the displayed differential eigenvalue $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}$. In the same scaling, $b_j=m_j\omega_j=\sqrt{c/a_j}$ and the normalized $n_j=0$ Gaussian becomes $(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}$; taking the product gives the stated ground representative. [A1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Each product Hermite function is a polynomial times a Gaussian, so it and all first derivatives have finite squared integrals after multiplication by any fixed polynomial. Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\chi_R(q)=\chi(q/R)$ with $\chi=1$ on $|q|\le1$, $\chi=0$ on $|q|\ge2$, and $|\nabla\chi_R|\le C/R$. Such a $\chi$ can be formed from $\eta(s)=e^{-1/s}$ for $s>0$ and $\eta(s)=0$ for $s\le0$, by taking $\chi(q)=\eta(4-|q|^2)/(\eta(4-|q|^2)+\eta(|q|^2-1))$. Then $0\le\chi_R\le1$ and $\chi_R\psi_{\mathbf n}\in C_c^\infty$. The weighted-function error is supported on $|q|>R$ and bounded in squared integral by the integrable tail $(c|q|^2+2)|\psi_{\mathbf n}|^2$, so its $L^2$ norm tends to zero. For each derivative,
$$\partial_j((1-\chi_R)\psi_{\mathbf n})=(1-\chi_R)\partial_j\psi_{\mathbf n}-(\partial_j\chi_R)\psi_{\mathbf n};$$
the first term tends to zero by its Gaussian tail and the second has norm at most $C\|\psi_{\mathbf n}\|_2/R$. Thus $\chi_R\psi_{\mathbf n}$ converges in the form norm, proving $\psi_{\mathbf n}\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 For $v\in C_c^\infty$, integration by parts and the eigenvalue identity in step 1.1 give
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(\psi_{\mathbf n},v)=(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2) \langle\psi_{\mathbf n},v\rangle.$$
The left side is continuous in the form norm of $v$ by Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and the right side is continuous since $\|v\|_2\le\|v\|_{Q_{\mathrm{osc}}}$. Density of $C_c^\infty$ in its defining completion extends the identity to every $v\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. Taking $v=\psi_{\mathbf m}$ proves that $\xi_{\mathbf n}:=(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2)^{-1/2}\psi_{\mathbf n}$ is orthonormal in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. If $u\in Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is orthogonal in this form inner product to every $\xi_{\mathbf n}$, conjugating the displayed identity gives $\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle=0$ for every $\mathbf n$. Completeness in $L^2$ from [F2] makes the image of $u$ zero, and the injective inclusion in [F1] makes $u=0$ in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$. Thus $(\xi_{\mathbf n})$ is complete there. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Parseval in $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ with the complete orthonormal family $(\xi_{\mathbf n})$ gives
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,u)=\sum_{\mathbf n}(\epsilon_{\mathbf n}+2) |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
Parseval in $L^2$ gives $\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{\mathbf n}|\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2$. Subtracting $2\|u\|_2^2$ from the first identity yields the asserted expansion of the unshifted oscillator form. [F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Positive injective compact polynomial form resolvent
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and use $Q$, $H_N$, $a$, and $W$ from
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]]. For each $f\in H_N$, let $Rf$ be
the unique vector of $Q$ satisfying
$$a(v,Rf)=\langle v,f\rangle_{H_N}\qquad(v\in Q),$$
and view $R$ as an operator $H_N\to H_N$ by the inclusion of
[[lem-qft-cube-poincare-compact-form-inclusion]]. Then $R$ is bounded, compact,
self-adjoint, positive, injective, and has dense range; moreover
$\|R\|\le\tfrac12$. This is the variational inverse of the shifted polynomial
form. It establishes compactness and dense range but does not itself assert a
differential-operator realization.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For fixed $f\in H_N$, the functional $v\mapsto\langle v,f\rangle_{H_N}$ is linear and satisfies $|\langle v,f\rangle|\le\|v\|_2\|f\|_2\le\|v\|_Q\|f\|_2$ by [F1] and Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus [F3] applied to the Hilbert space $(Q,a)$ gives a unique $Rf\in Q$ with the stated variational identity. For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$, conjugate-linearity in the second argument gives $a(v,\alpha Rf+\beta Rg)=\langle v,\alpha f+\beta g\rangle$, so uniqueness makes $R$ linear. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given]

2.1 Taking $v=Rf$ in the identity gives $\|Rf\|_Q^2=a(Rf,Rf)=\langle Rf,f\rangle$. Hence $\|Rf\|_Q^2\le\|Rf\|_2\|f\|_2\le\|Rf\|_Q\|f\|_2$, so $\|Rf\|_Q\le\|f\|_2$ (with the zero case immediate). Consequently $R:H_N\to H_N$ is bounded by [F5]. [step 1.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra]

2.2 The same identity and $a(Rf,Rf)\ge2\|Rf\|_2^2$ give $2\|Rf\|_2^2\le\|Rf\|_2\|f\|_2$; division when $Rf\ne0$ yields $\|R\|\le\tfrac12$. If $Rf=0$, the variational identity says $\langle v,f\rangle=0$ for every $v\in Q$; since $Q$ is dense in $H_N$ by [F1], continuity of the inner product gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$. Thus $R$ is injective. [step 1.1, F1, F4, algebra]

2.3 For $f,g\in H_N$, the variational identity and conjugate symmetry of $a$ yield $\langle Rf,g\rangle=a(Rf,Rg)=\langle f,Rg\rangle$, so $R$ is self-adjoint by [F7]. Also $\langle Rf,f\rangle=a(Rf,Rf)\ge0$, so it is positive. [step 1.1, F1, F7, algebra]

3.1 The map $f\mapsto Rf$ is bounded from $H_N$ into $Q$ by step 2.1, and the inclusion $J:Q\to H_N$ is compact by [F2]. Therefore for every bounded $B\subseteq H_N$, $R(B)=J(R(B))$ has compact closure, which is exactly compactness by [F6]. [step 2.1, F2, F6]

4.1 If $z\perp\operatorname{ran}R$, then $\langle Rf,z\rangle=0$ for every $f\in H_N$. Self-adjointness from step 2.3 gives $\langle f,Rz\rangle=0$ for every $f$, so $Rz=0$ and step 2.2 gives $z=0$. Thus $(\operatorname{ran}R)^\perp=\{0\}$, and [F8] gives $\overline{\operatorname{ran}R}=(\operatorname{ran}R)^{\perp\perp}=\{0\}^\perp=H_N$. Therefore $R$ has dense range. [step 2.2, step 2.3, F8] ∎

items.title: Self-adjoint unbounded polynomial interaction at fixed regulator
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and the data of
[[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]. Its variational operator $R$
is compact, self-adjoint, positive, and injective on the infinite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space $H_N$. Let $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ be its positive eigenvalues
in nonincreasing order, with multiplicity, and choose corresponding
orthonormal eigenvectors $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$. Put
$E_n:=\mu_n^{-1}-1$ and define
$$D(S):=\left\{u=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\psi_n\in H_N:\sum_{n\ge1}E_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad Su:=\sum_{n\ge1}E_nc_n\psi_n.$$
The series for $u$ converges in $H_N$ by the Hilbert-space expansion theorem.
Then $S$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\langle Su,u\rangle\ge\|u\|_2^2$
for every $u\in D(S)$; also $(S+I)^{-1}=R$ is compact. For every
$u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
$$Su=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Wu.$$
Consequently $h:=S-(C_0+1)I$, on the same domain, is a self-adjoint realization
of the differential expression in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]] and satisfies
$\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$ for every $u\in D(h)$.
It has compact resolvent, meaning that for some $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
$h-zI:D(h)\to H_N$ is bijective with bounded inverse on $H_N$, and that
inverse is compact; here $z=-(C_0+2)$ and $(h+(C_0+2)I)^{-1}=R$. Put
$\lambda_n:=E_n-C_0-1$, the eigenvalues of $h$; equivalently,
$$D(h)=\left\{u=\sum_nc_n\psi_n:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $u\in Q$,
$$a(u,u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(E_n+1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2,\qquad q_h(u):=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The lowest eigenvalue is attained and has finite multiplicity. This selects a
form realization; it does not assert that the differential expression on
$C_c^\infty$ is essentially self-adjoint or that it has no other self-adjoint
extensions.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1], $R$ is compact and self-adjoint. Applying [F2] and using $\ker R=\{0\}$ shows that the closed span of its nonzero eigenspaces is all of $H_N$. If $R\psi=\mu\psi$ with $\psi\ne0$, then $\mu\|\psi\|^2=\langle R\psi,\psi\rangle\ge0$ by positivity, while injectivity rules out $\mu=0$; hence every nonzero eigenvalue is positive. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 The domains defined by the squared coefficient sums for $E_n$ and $\lambda_n=E_n-(C_0+1)$ coincide. Indeed
$$\lambda_n^2\le2E_n^2+2(C_0+1)^2,\qquad E_n^2\le2\lambda_n^2+2(C_0+1)^2.$$
Multiplying by $|c_n|^2$ and summing preserves finiteness in both directions because $\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|u\|_2^2<\infty$ by [F4]. This proves the displayed coefficient-domain description of $D(h)$. [F4, algebra]

2.1 Each eigenspace is finite-dimensional by [F2], and so has an orthonormal basis by [F3]. The set of nonzero eigenvalues is at most countable, and [A1] selects these finite bases; their union is an orthonormal family whose closed span is $H_N$ by step 1.1. The space is infinite-dimensional: the indicators of the pairwise disjoint unit cubes $[r,r+1)\times[0,1)^{N-1}$, $r\in\mathbb N$, are nonzero mutually orthogonal $L^2$ vectors. Thus the family can be indexed by $n\ge1$. The bound $\|R\|\le\tfrac12$ gives $0<\mu_n\le\tfrac12$ and $E_n\ge1$. The compact spectral theorem says only finitely many eigenvalues satisfy $\mu\ge\varepsilon$ for each $\varepsilon>0$; recursively taking a largest remaining eigenvalue (which exists because above half its positive supremum there are only finitely many) orders them nonincreasingly with multiplicity and gives $\mu_n\to0$, hence $E_n\to\infty$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The family $(\psi_n)$ is complete by step 1.1, so [F4] gives $u=\sum_n\langle u,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n$ in norm for every $u\in H_N$ and Parseval. In particular $D(S)$ is dense because it contains all finite linear combinations of the $\psi_n$. Since each $E_n$ is real, the diagonal formula for $S$ gives $\langle Su,v\rangle=\langle u,Sv\rangle$ for finite sums, and then for all $u,v\in D(S)$ by [F7] and convergence of the coefficient series; thus $S$ is symmetric. For $u\in D(S)$ with coefficients $c_n$, Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] makes $\sum_nE_n|c_n|^2$ absolutely convergent, and step 2.1 gives $E_n\ge1$, so $\langle Su,u\rangle=\sum_nE_n|c_n|^2\ge\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|u\|_2^2$. [F4, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 To compute the adjoint domain, let $v=\sum_nd_n\psi_n\in D(S^*)$ and write $S^*v=z=\sum_nz_n\psi_n$. Testing the adjoint identity on each $\psi_n$ gives $z_n=E_nd_n$. Because $z\in H_N$, Parseval gives $\sum_nE_n^2|d_n|^2<\infty$, so $v\in D(S)$. Conversely, if this sum is finite, then $z:=\sum_nE_nd_n\psi_n\in H_N$ and the coefficient identity $\langle Su,v\rangle=\langle u,z\rangle$ holds first for finite sums and then for every $u\in D(S)$ by [F7]; hence $v\in D(S^*)$ and $S^*v=Sv$. Therefore $D(S^*)=D(S)$ and $S^*=S$ as operators; by the unbounded self-adjointness definition in [F5], $S$ is self-adjoint. [F4, F5, F7, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 On each $\psi_n$, $(S+I)^{-1}\psi_n=(E_n+1)^{-1}\psi_n=\mu_n\psi_n=R\psi_n$. Both sides are bounded operators on $H_N$ and agree on the span of the complete family, so they agree on all of $H_N$. Thus $(S+I)^{-1}=R$, which is compact by [F1]. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 The variational identity for $R$, applied to $f=\psi_n$, gives $a(v,R\psi_n)=\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ for every $v\in Q$. Since $R\psi_n=\mu_n\psi_n$ and $\mu_n>0$, each $\psi_n$ lies in $Q$ and
$$a(v,\psi_n)=\mu_n^{-1}\langle v,\psi_n\rangle.$$
Thus $\xi_n:=\sqrt{\mu_n}\,\psi_n$ is an orthonormal family in $Q$. If $v\in Q$ is orthogonal in $a$ to every $\xi_n$, the displayed identity makes all $H_N$ coefficients $\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ zero. The $H_N$ completeness of $(\psi_n)$ and injectivity of $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ force $v=0$ in $Q$. Hence $(\xi_n)$ is complete in $Q$, and Parseval in $(Q,a)$ gives
$$a(v,v)=\sum_n\mu_n^{-1}|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2=\sum_n(E_n+1)|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
[F1, F4, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.2, algebra]

5.2 Let $u\in C_c^\infty$ and set $f:=(-\sum_ja_j\partial_j^2+W+1)u\in H_N$. Integration by parts gives $a(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for $v\in C_c^\infty$; both sides are continuous in $v$ for the $Q$ norm by [F7], and $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $Q$, so the identity holds for all $v\in Q$. It is the defining variational identity for $Rf$, and uniqueness in [F1] gives $Rf=u$. Hence $u\in\operatorname{ran}R=D(S)$ and $(S+I)u=f$, so $Su=-\sum_ja_j\partial_j^2u+Wu$. [F1, F7, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 Parseval in $H_N$ gives $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_n|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2$. Subtracting $(C_0+2)$ times this identity from step 5.1 yields the claimed formula for $q_h(v)$, because $E_n+1-(C_0+2)=E_n-C_0-1=\lambda_n$. [step 5.1, F4, algebra]

6.2 If $u\in D(h)=D(S)$ and $c_n=\langle u,\psi_n\rangle$, then $\sum_nE_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$ by the definition of $D(S)$. Since $E_n\ge1$, $E_n+1\le2E_n^2$, so $\sum_n(E_n+1)|c_n|^2<\infty$. Step 5.1 therefore gives $u\in Q$. Thus every eigenvector, and indeed every operator-domain vector, belongs to the form domain. [F2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Subtracting the real scalar $(C_0+1)I$ preserves self-adjointness on the same domain, and $E_n\ge1$ gives eigenvalues $\lambda_n=E_n-C_0-1\ge-C_0$. For $u\in D(h)$, the diagonal expansion and Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] make $\langle hu,u\rangle=\sum_n\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2$ absolutely convergent; Parseval then gives $\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$. The lowest eigenvalue corresponds to the largest eigenvalue $\mu_1$ of $R$; its eigenspace is nonzero and finite-dimensional by [F2]. Since $W=V+C_0+1$, step 5.2 shows that $h=S-(C_0+1)I$ extends the specified polynomial differential expression. Finally $h+(C_0+2)I=S+I$, whose inverse is the compact operator $R$ by step 4.2. These statements establish the declared realization and all listed scope limits. [F1, F2, F7, step 2.1, step 4.2, step 5.2] ∎

Richard S. Laugesen, Spectral Theory of Partial Differential Equations — Lecture Notes, Chapter 4, pp.27–32

items.title: Global unitary evolution at fixed finite regulator
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and let $h$ be the self-adjoint operator of
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]], with complete orthonormal
eigenfamily $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$ and real eigenvalues
$\lambda_n=E_n-C_0-1$. For $t\in\mathbb R$ define
$$U(t)f:=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-it\lambda_n}\langle f,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n \qquad(f\in H_N).$$
Then the series converges in $H_N$ for every $f$; $U(t)$ is unitary,
$U(0)=I$, $U(s+t)=U(s)U(t)$, and $t\mapsto U(t)f$ is norm-continuous for
every $f$. Its norm derivative at any $t$ exists exactly for $f\in D(h)$, and
then
$$\frac{d}{dt}U(t)f=-i\,hU(t)f.$$
This is a mathematical one-parameter group with a dimensionless real
parameter; it makes no physical unit or empirical claim.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $f\in H_N$, its coefficients $c_n=\langle f,\psi_n\rangle$, and the real sequence $(\lambda_n)$.

1.1 Parseval gives $\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|f\|^2$. Since $|e^{-it\lambda_n}|=1$, the finite partial sums defining $U(t)f$ are Cauchy in $H_N$, so converge; Parseval gives $\|U(t)f\|^2=\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|f\|^2$. The coefficient formula shows $U(-t)U(t)f=f=U(t)U(-t)f$ and $U(s)U(t)f=U(s+t)f$, first on finite sums and then on all of $H_N$ by norm convergence and the norm bound. Thus $U(t)$ is a surjective isometry, hence unitary, and $U(0)=I$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Fix $s\in\mathbb R$ and $f\in H_N$. Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite set $F\subset\mathbb N$ with $\sum_{n\notin F}|c_n|^2<\varepsilon^2/64$, possible by convergence of the nonnegative series in [F2]. The norm of the difference on the complement is at most $2(\sum_{n\notin F}|c_n|^2)^{1/2}<\varepsilon/4$. On the finite set $F$, each scalar $e^{-it\lambda_n}$ is continuous in $t$, so the finite partial difference has norm below $3\varepsilon/4$ for $t$ sufficiently close to $s$. The triangle inequality proves $\|U(t)f-U(s)f\|<\varepsilon$, establishing strong continuity. [F2, algebra]

1.3 Let $f\in D(h)$, so $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$. Since $|e^{-it\lambda_n}|=1$, $U(t)f$ has the same finite weighted coefficient sum and belongs to $D(h)$. For $r\ne0$,
$$\frac{U(t+r)f-U(t)f}{r} =\sum_ne^{-it\lambda_n}\frac{e^{-ir\lambda_n}-1}{r}c_n\psi_n.$$
The scalar integral identity $e^{-ir\lambda}-1=\int_0^r(-i\lambda)e^{-is\lambda}\,ds$ gives $|(e^{-ir\lambda}-1)/r|\le|\lambda|$. Thus the difference quotient coefficients are dominated in square sum by $\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2$. On each finite set they converge to $-i\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n$; choosing a finite set with small tail in that dominating series and then taking $r\to0$ proves convergence in $H_N$ to $-i\sum_n\lambda_ne^{-it\lambda_n}c_n\psi_n=-ihU(t)f$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Conversely, suppose the norm derivative at $t=0$ exists and equals $g\in H_N$. Continuity of the coefficient functional $v\mapsto\langle v,\psi_n\rangle$ from [F3] makes its value on the difference quotient converge to $-i\lambda_nc_n$. Hence $\langle g,\psi_n\rangle=-i\lambda_nc_n$ for every $n$. Parseval for $g$ implies $\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2=\|g\|^2<\infty$, so $f\in D(h)$ by [F1]. If the derivative exists at any other $t$, the same coefficient argument multiplies each coefficient by a unit phase and yields the identical summability condition. Thus the differentiability domain is exactly $D(h)$ at every $t$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎

items.title: Finite-regulator Gibbs trace and bounded expectations
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and use the finite-mode data, form domain $Q$, and
self-adjoint $h$ from [[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let
$\lambda_0\le\lambda_1\le\cdots$ be its eigenvalues repeated with
multiplicity, and let $\psi_k$ be a corresponding orthonormal eigenbasis. For
$\beta>0$ define the finite-rank truncations
$$\rho_{\beta,M}f:=\sum_{k=0}^M e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\psi_k.$$
The proof establishes their operator-norm limit $\rho_\beta$, with action
$$\rho_\beta f:=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\psi_k.$$
Put $\alpha_j:=\sqrt{a_jc}$ and let the oscillator eigenvalues
$\epsilon_k$ be the nondecreasing ordering, with multiplicity, of
$$\epsilon_{\mathbf n}=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\alpha_j, \qquad\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N.$$
Then $\rho_\beta$ is positive trace class and its trace
$$Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta)=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}$$
satisfies the finite bound
$$0<Z_\beta\le e^{\beta C_0} \prod_{j=1}^N\frac{e^{-\beta\alpha_j}}{1-e^{-2\beta\alpha_j}}<\infty.$$
For every bounded linear operator $B:H_N\to H_N$, the normalized trace
expectation is well defined and
$$Z_\beta^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B) =Z_\beta^{-1}\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k} \langle B\psi_k,\psi_k\rangle,$$
with absolute convergence. This is a finite-$N$ mathematical trace result;
it assumes no statistical data and makes no continuum-limit claim.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $N\ge1$, $a_j,c>0$, $V(q)\ge c|q|^2-C_0$, the interacting form, and $\beta>0$.

1.1 Each $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}$ is finite, and only finitely many multi-indices have $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\le M$ for any real $M$: for $M\ge0$, that inequality bounds every nonnegative integer $n_j$ by $M/(2\alpha_j)$, while for $M<0$ there are none. Fix the explicit degree-then-lexicographic enumeration of $\mathbb N_0^N$. Recursively, among the remaining tuples choose one of least energy, breaking a tie by that fixed enumeration; such a least energy exists because below the energy of the first remaining tuple there are only finitely many candidates. Every tuple is eventually listed, since only finitely many tuples have energy at most its energy. This gives the nondecreasing list $(\epsilon_k)_{k\ge0}$ with multiplicity. [F2, algebra]

1.2 On $C_c^\infty$, the shifted interacting form has weight $V+C_0+2\ge c|q|^2+2$, so it dominates the shifted oscillator form from [F2]. Therefore a Cauchy sequence in $Q$ is Cauchy in the oscillator form norm; the identity map extends to a continuous map $Q\to Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, with the same $L^2$ representative because both completions inject into $H_N$ by [F3]. Subtracting the shifts in the two form norms gives
$$q_h(u)=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2\ge q_{\mathrm{osc}}(u)-C_0\|u\|_2^2\qquad(u\in Q).$$
[F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Fix $k\ge0$ and let $L_k=\operatorname{span}\{\psi_0,\ldots,\psi_k\}$. The linear map from $L_k$ to the span of the first $k$ oscillator eigenvectors, sending $u$ to its $k$ oscillator coefficients, has a nonzero kernel because $\dim L_k=k+1>k$. Choose $u\ne0$ in that kernel. Since $u$ lies in the span of the first $k+1$ interacting eigenvectors, [F1] gives $q_h(u)\le\lambda_k\|u\|_2^2$. Its oscillator coefficients at indices below $k$ vanish, so [F2] gives $q_{\mathrm{osc}}(u)\ge\epsilon_k\|u\|_2^2$. Step 1.2 now yields $\lambda_k\|u\|_2^2\ge q_h(u)\ge(\epsilon_k-C_0)\|u\|_2^2$, hence
$$\lambda_k\ge\epsilon_k-C_0.$$
This argument also covers $k=0$, when the span of zero oscillator vectors is $\{0\}$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 By step 2.1 and $\beta>0$,
$$\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\beta\lambda_k} \le e^{\beta C_0}\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N} e^{-\beta\epsilon_{\mathbf n}} =e^{\beta C_0}\prod_{j=1}^N \left(\sum_{n_j\ge0}e^{-\beta(2n_j+1)\alpha_j}\right) =e^{\beta C_0}\prod_{j=1}^N \frac{e^{-\beta\alpha_j}}{1-e^{-2\beta\alpha_j}}.$$
The factorization follows first for finite rectangular sums by distributivity and then by increasing limits of nonnegative sums. Each denominator is positive because $0<e^{-2\beta\alpha_j}<1$. The lower bound $Z_\beta>0$ follows from its positive ground term. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The coefficients satisfy $0<e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\le e^{\beta C_0}$ by [F1]. For each $f$, Parseval makes the finite partial sums in the defining series for $\rho_\beta f$ Cauchy in $H_N$, so the series converges; its coefficient formula gives linearity and $\|\rho_\beta f\|_2\le e^{\beta C_0}\|f\|_2$. Moreover Parseval gives
$$\|\rho_\beta-\rho_{\beta,M}\|\le\sup_{k>M}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\longrightarrow0,$$
since $\lambda_k\to+\infty$ and $\beta>0$. Each truncation is finite rank and hence compact by [F10], so the operator-norm limit $\rho_\beta$ is compact by [F11]. The same convergence makes its rank-one partial sums converge in operator norm, and their coefficient sum is $\sum_ke^{-\beta\lambda_k}=Z_\beta<\infty$; thus $\rho_\beta$ is trace class by [F4]. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F10, F11, F12, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Since each $e^{-\beta\lambda_k}$ is real, the Fourier expansion [F12] gives
$$\langle\rho_\beta f,g\rangle=\sum_k e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle f,\psi_k\rangle\langle\psi_k,g\rangle=\langle f,\rho_\beta g\rangle$$
for all $f,g\in H_N$; the series is absolutely convergent by Cauchy--Schwarz
for the coefficient sequences and boundedness of the weights. Thus
$\rho_\beta$ is self-adjoint. It is positive because
$$\langle\rho_\beta f,f\rangle =\sum_ke^{-\beta\lambda_k}|\langle f,\psi_k\rangle|^2\ge0.$$
The defining series gives $\rho_\beta\psi_k=e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\psi_k$. If $\rho_\beta x=\mu x$, taking Fourier coefficients shows $(e^{-\beta\lambda_k}-\mu)\langle x,\psi_k\rangle=0$ for every $k$. Completeness [F1, F12] then implies that every nonzero eigenspace is exactly the span of basis vectors with the corresponding repeated diagonal value; since every diagonal value is positive, $0$ is not an eigenvalue. Thus the eigenvalues with multiplicity are precisely $(e^{-\beta\lambda_k})$, and [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta)=Z_\beta$. For bounded $B$, each $\rho_{\beta,M}B$ is finite rank and hence compact by [F10], while
$$\|\rho_{\beta,M}B-\rho_\beta B\|\le\|\rho_{\beta,M}-\rho_\beta\|\,\|B\|\to0$$
by step 4.1. Therefore $\rho_\beta B$ is compact by [F11]. The functional $x\mapsto\langle Bx,\psi_k\rangle$ is linear and has norm at most $\|B\|$ by [F9] and [F8]. By [F6] it is represented by a vector $w_k$ with $\|w_k\|\le\|B\|$ and $\langle Bx,\psi_k\rangle=\langle x,w_k\rangle$. Hence
$$\rho_\beta Bx=\sum_k\langle x,w_k\rangle e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\psi_k.$$
The partial sums converge in operator norm: the norm of the tail after $M$ is at most $\|B\|\sum_{k>M}e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\to0$ by step 3.1. This nuclear representation has coefficient sum at most $\|B\|Z_\beta$. Since $\rho_\beta B$ is compact as shown above, [F4] gives that it is trace class. Its basis trace in $(\psi_k)$ is absolutely convergent and equals the trace by [F7]. The $k$th diagonal entry is
$$\langle \rho_\beta B\psi_k,\psi_k\rangle =e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\langle B\psi_k,\psi_k\rangle,$$
so this basis sum is the asserted numerator. Each term is bounded in modulus by $e^{-\beta\lambda_k}\|B\|$ by [F8] and [F9], giving the stated absolute bound. Division by $Z_\beta>0$ proves the expectation formula. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, F12, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Ground eigenvalue as the form variational infimum
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice and use $Q$, $q_h$, and the operator $h$ from
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Let $\lambda_1$ be the least
eigenvalue of $h$. Then
$$\inf\{q_h(u):u\in Q,\ \|u\|_2=1\}=\lambda_1.$$
The infimum is attained by every normalized vector in the lowest eigenspace;
no simplicity or nondegeneracy is assumed.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $u\in Q$ and the ordered real eigenvalue list.

1.1 Since $\lambda_n\ge\lambda_1$ for every $n$, [A1], [F1] and [F2] imply
$$q_h(u)-\lambda_1\|u\|_2^2 =\sum_n(\lambda_n-\lambda_1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2\ge0.$$
Thus every unit vector in $Q$ has form value at least $\lambda_1$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 A normalized eigenvector $\psi_1$ belongs to $D(h)\subseteq Q$ by
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]], has norm one, and its sole
nonzero coefficient is at an eigenvalue $\lambda_1$. Therefore
$q_h(\psi_1)=\lambda_1$, so the lower bound is attained and equals the
infimum. If the lowest eigenspace has dimension greater than one, the same
coefficient calculation applies to every normalized vector in it. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Fixed finite-mode results do not establish a continuum limit
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
In [[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]], the regulator is one fixed
finite mode count $N$ and one fixed polynomial on $\mathbb R^N$. The self-adjoint
and compact-resolvent conclusions of
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]] concern that fixed Hilbert space
and form realization. They assert no continuum or infinite-volume limit. Here
“continuum limit” means a limit of a specified family of finite-regulator
objects as a cutoff parameter changes, together with an identified comparison
space and convergence notion. No such family or convergence structure is part
of the two cited items. This scope note does not assert that a continuum limit
does not exist.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** [F1] and [F2].

1.1 The hypotheses in [F1] specify a single integer $N$, a single coordinate space $\mathbb R^N$, and a single potential $V$; they contain no indexed family with varying cutoff. [A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 A convergence assertion for varying cutoffs requires at least a family of objects, a common comparison space or maps between the spaces, and a convergence relation. Neither those data nor a limiting object occur in [F1] or [F2]. Therefore the theorems establish only the stated fixed-$N$ operator properties. The absence of those hypotheses is not a proof of nonexistence of a limit in a separately specified model. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: One-mode quartic ground-energy increment bound
items.design_state: Authored draft with complete local argument; independent review remains pending.
items.statement:
Assume $a>0$, $m>0$, and $\lambda\ge0$, all real mathematical parameters.
For $N=1$ take the polynomial
$$V_\lambda(q)=\frac{m^2}{2}q^2+\lambda q^4$$
and the differential expression $h_\lambda=-a\,d^2/dq^2+V_\lambda(q)$ with
the form realization of [[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]]. Write
$E_g(\lambda)$ for its least eigenvalue. Then
$$0\le E_g(\lambda)-E_g(0)\le\frac{3a\lambda}{2m^2}.$$
The parameters are mathematical and dimensionless here; no physical mass,
unit, measurement, or continuum claim is made.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** $a,m>0$, $\lambda\ge0$, and the forms $q_0,q_\lambda$.

1.1 Write $a_\lambda=q_\lambda+2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ for the shifted form inner product of the $\lambda$ completion. On $C_c^\infty$, $V_\lambda\ge V_0$ gives $a_\lambda(u,u)\ge a_0(u,u)$, so a $Q_\lambda$-Cauchy sequence is $Q_0$-Cauchy and the identity extends continuously to $Q_\lambda\to Q_0$ with the same $L^2$ representative. The unshifted forms $q_\lambda=a_\lambda-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ and $q_0=a_0-2\|\cdot\|_2^2$ are continuous on their respective form spaces. For any $u\in Q_\lambda$, approximate it in $Q_\lambda$ by $u_r\in C_c^\infty$; then $q_\lambda(u_r)\ge q_0(u_r)$ for every $r$, and continuity of both forms gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)$ in the limit. For normalized $u\in Q_\lambda$, [F3] then gives $q_\lambda(u)\ge q_0(u)\ge E_g(0)$. Taking the infimum yields $E_g(\lambda)\ge E_g(0)$. [A1, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 The Gaussian $\phi_b$ from [F2] and its derivative are polynomial times a Gaussian. For cutoffs $\chi_R$ as in the cutoff construction of
[[lem-qft-hermite-oscillator-research-supplier]], $\chi_R\phi_b\in C_c^\infty$
converges to $\phi_b$ in the $\lambda$ form norm: the derivative error is
$(1-\chi_R)\phi_b'-(\chi_R')\phi_b$, whose first term has vanishing Gaussian
tail and whose second has norm at most $C\|\phi_b\|_2/R$; the weighted error
has squared magnitude bounded by $(m^2q^2/2+\lambda q^4+2)|\phi_b|^2$, an
integrable polynomial-Gaussian tail. Thus $\phi_b\in Q_\lambda$. [A1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Let $\mathbb E_b[g]:=\int g(q)\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2}\,dq$. The Hermite
ground function in [F2] is normalized, so $\mathbb E_b[1]=1$. On any compact
interval of positive $b$ values, the derivatives of the integrands through
order two are bounded by a constant times $(1+|q|^4)e^{-b_*q^2}$ for some
$b_*>0$, which is integrable; [F5] therefore permits differentiation under the
integral. Differentiating $\mathbb E_b[1]=1$ gives
$$0=\mathbb E_b\!\left[\frac1{2b}-q^2\right],\qquad \mathbb E_b[q^2]=\frac1{2b}.$$
Differentiating the second identity and using
$\partial_b(\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2})=(\frac1{2b}-q^2)\sqrt{b/\pi}e^{-bq^2}$ gives
$$-\frac1{2b^2}=\mathbb E_b\!\left[q^2\left(\frac1{2b}-q^2\right)\right] =\frac1{4b^2}-\mathbb E_b[q^4],$$
so $\mathbb E_b[q^4]=3/(4b^2)$. Since $\phi_b'=-bq\phi_b$, this gives
$\|\phi_b'\|_2^2=b/2$. Hence
$$\|\phi_b\|_2^2=1,\quad \|\phi_b'\|_2^2=b/2,\quad \int q^2|\phi_b|^2=1/(2b),\quad\int q^4|\phi_b|^2=3/(4b^2).$$
The unperturbed form value
is $ab/2+m^2/(4b)=m\sqrt{a/2}=E_g(0)$, using $b=m/\sqrt{2a}$, and the quartic
contribution is $3\lambda/(4b^2)=3a\lambda/(2m^2)$. The variational bound
[F3] applied to this normalized vector yields
$$E_g(\lambda)\le E_g(0)+\frac{3a\lambda}{2m^2}.$$
Combining with step 1.1 proves both inequalities, including $\lambda=0$.
[A1, F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: Finite Euclidean quartic interacting measure

references.title: David Skinner, Advanced Quantum Field Theory, Chapter 2, “QFT in Zero Dimensions” (University of Cambridge Part III lecture notes)
Nima Moshayedi, Quantum Field Theory and Functional Integrals (lecture notes, arXiv:1902.08652)

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite and let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ matrix; positive-semidefinite means $u^{\mathsf T}Cu\ge0$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^N$. The centered multivariate normal Borel probability law with covariance $C$ is $\gamma_C:=N_N(0,C)$ as defined by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: every linear projection $q\mapsto u^{\mathsf T}q$ has scalar normal law $N(0,u^{\mathsf T}Cu)$, and the law exists even when $C$ is singular. Here $N(0,\sigma^2)$ is the law specified in [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], with density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ for the standard case.

Let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, meaning $U$ is a polynomial and $U(sq)=s^4U(q)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$ and $q\in\mathbb R^N$. For a coupling $\lambda\ge0$, define the partition integral and its weighted measure by

$$Z_{C,U}(\lambda):=\int_{\mathbb R^N}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q),\qquad \nu_{C,U,\lambda}(A):=\int_Ae^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q)$$

for Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb R^N$. Whenever $0<Z_{C,U}(\lambda)<\infty$, the **finite Euclidean interacting measure** is the Borel probability measure

$$d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}(q):=Z_{C,U}(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U(q)}\,d\gamma_C(q).$$

For a polynomial $P:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R$ with finite integral, write $\langle P\rangle_{C,U,\lambda}:=\int P\,d\mu_{C,U,\lambda}$. The exact supplier [[thm-qft-finite-euclidean-polynomial-measure]] proves that $Z_{C,U}(\lambda)$ is positive and finite and that every polynomial insertion is integrable. This is a Borel measure on finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^N$; it is not a measure on distributions on continuum Euclidean spacetime and does not by itself assert reflection positivity or reconstruction of a continuum field.

items.title: Finite Gaussian normalization and Wick moments

references.title: David Skinner, Advanced Quantum Field Theory, Chapter 2, “QFT in Zero Dimensions” (University of Cambridge Part III lecture notes)
Nima Moshayedi, Quantum Field Theory and Functional Integrals (lecture notes, arXiv:1902.08652)

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite $N\times N$ covariance matrix, and let $Q\sim\gamma_C=N_N(0,C)$ be the law of [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]]. For $k\ge0$ and vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in\mathbb R^N$, every product $\prod_{j=1}^k(u_j^{\mathsf T}Q)$ is integrable. For $k=0$ its expectation is $1$. If $k$ is odd, its expectation is $0$; if $k=2m$, then

$$\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j=1}^{2m}u_j^{\mathsf T}Q\right]=\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Pair}(2m)}\prod_{\{a,b\}\in\pi}u_a^{\mathsf T}Cu_b,$$

where $\operatorname{Pair}(2m)$ is the finite set of partitions of $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ into unordered two-element subsets. Thus every polynomial in $Q$ has a finite absolute moment, computed by finitely many covariance pairings.

items.title: Actual finite Euclidean polynomial measure and moments

references.title: David Skinner, Advanced Quantum Field Theory, Chapter 2, “QFT in Zero Dimensions” (University of Cambridge Part III lecture notes)
Nima Moshayedi, Quantum Field Theory and Functional Integrals (lecture notes, arXiv:1902.08652)

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $N\ge1$ be finite, let $C$ be a real symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance matrix, let $\gamma_C=N_N(0,C)$, let $U:\mathbb R^N\to[0,\infty)$ be a real homogeneous quartic polynomial, and let $\lambda\ge0$. Define $Z(\lambda)=\int e^{-\lambda U}\,d\gamma_C$ and $N_P(\lambda)=\int P e^{-\lambda U}\,d\gamma_C$ for every real polynomial $P$.

Then $0<Z(\lambda)\le1$, and $\mu_\lambda:=Z(\lambda)^{-1}e^{-\lambda U}\gamma_C$ is a Borel probability measure. Every polynomial insertion is integrable under $\mu_\lambda$. For each integer $r\ge0$,

$$Z^{(r)}(\lambda)=(-1)^r\int U^r e^{-\lambda U}\,d\gamma_C,\qquad N_P^{(r)}(\lambda)=(-1)^r\int P U^r e^{-\lambda U}\,d\gamma_C$$

for $\lambda>0$, with continuous right derivatives of every finite order at $\lambda=0$. No continuum field measure is asserted.

items.title: Finite covariance Wick normal powers

references.title: David Skinner, Advanced Quantum Field Theory, Chapter 2, “QFT in Zero Dimensions” (University of Cambridge Part III lecture notes)
Nima Moshayedi, Quantum Field Theory and Functional Integrals (lecture notes, arXiv:1902.08652)

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $Q\sim N_N(0,C)$ be the centered finite-dimensional Gaussian vector of [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]], and write $C_{jj}=\mathbb E[Q_j^2]\ge0$ for the variance of its $j$th coordinate. For each coordinate $j$ and integer $n\ge0$, its **finite covariance Wick normal power** is the polynomial $:Q_j^n:_C$ defined by the formal generating identity

$$\exp\!\left(tQ_j-\frac12t^2C_{jj}\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}:Q_j^n:_C\,\frac{t^n}{n!}.$$

Equivalently,

$$:Q_j^n:_C=n!\sum_{s=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{(-C_{jj}/2)^sQ_j^{n-2s}}{s!(n-2s)!},\qquad :Q_j^4:_C=Q_j^4-6C_{jj}Q_j^2+3C_{jj}^2.$$

This is a finite-dimensional polynomial definition; it does not define a product of unsmeared continuum fields.

items.title: Finite interacting asymptotic Wick expansion with remainder

references.title: David Skinner, Advanced Quantum Field Theory, Chapter 2, “QFT in Zero Dimensions” (University of Cambridge Part III lecture notes)
Nima Moshayedi, Quantum Field Theory and Functional Integrals (lecture notes, arXiv:1902.08652)

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses and notation of [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]]. Let $P\in\mathbb R[q_1,\ldots,q_N]$, $Z(\lambda)=\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[e^{-\lambda U}]$, $N_P(\lambda)=\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[P e^{-\lambda U}]$, and $\langle P\rangle_\lambda=N_P(\lambda)/Z(\lambda)$. For every integer $M\ge0$,

$$Z(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^M z_j\lambda^j+R_{M,1}(\lambda),\qquad z_j=\frac{(-1)^j}{j!}\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[U^j],\qquad |R_{M,1}(\lambda)|\le\frac{\lambda^{M+1}}{(M+1)!}\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[U^{M+1}]$$

for $\lambda\ge0$. Likewise,

$$N_P(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^M a_j(P)\lambda^j+R_{M,P}(\lambda),\qquad a_j(P)=\frac{(-1)^j}{j!}\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[PU^j],\qquad |R_{M,P}(\lambda)|\le\frac{\lambda^{M+1}}{(M+1)!}\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[|P|U^{M+1}].$$

Define $b_0(P)=a_0(P)$ and, for $m\ge1$, $b_m(P)=a_m(P)-\sum_{j=1}^m z_jb_{m-j}(P)$. Then

$$\langle P\rangle_\lambda=\sum_{j=0}^M b_j(P)\lambda^j+O(\lambda^{M+1})\quad\text{as }\lambda\downarrow0.$$

Every coefficient is computed from finitely many Gaussian polynomial moments and hence from finitely many covariance pairings by [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]]. These estimates hold separately for each finite $M$; they do not assert convergence of the infinite formal series or any continuum limit.
